# Answer key — Chapter 09: Security monitoring and IDS {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-09-monitoring-cloud · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The chapter states that attacks on cloud systems are often scripted, so data
can be stolen or exposed within seconds or minutes of the first break-in
(CSA, 2024, p. 262), which is why detection works in real time where
possible; a, c and d are invented mechanisms.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-09-events-alerts-telemetry · basic)* — **Correct: c.**
Target's malware-detection system generated alerts, but nobody acted on
them in time — the callout's stated lesson is that an alert nobody responds
to is no better than no alert, which is why the response process of
Session 12 exists; a, b and d are not the point the chapter draws.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-09-detection · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
@def-ids and the following paragraph: the IDS is passive and out-of-band,
observing a copy and alerting; the IPS is inline and can block, but a false
positive then blocks a real user; a reverses them, c is false (either may
use signature or anomaly), d is false (both are increasingly cloud
services).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-09-detection · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"a sequence of detection mechanisms applied to incoming streams, each
narrowing the data further, from broadly suspicious to confirmed threat";
"it turns many events into few alerts and it manages cost, since most raw
logs stay cheaply where they are and only pertinent alerts and selected
logs go to the security team" (any phrasing naming the successive narrowing
and both purposes: detection quality and cost).

**Q5** *(tests @sec-09-detection · basic)* — **Accepted answers:** any two
of: "unauthorised API calls", "management console logins without MFA",
"any IAM policy change", "any use of the root account", "unusual IAM or
network security activity, especially in unused regions".

**Q6** *(tests @sec-09-detection · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
Comer's point: a cloud-native application starts and stops instances all
the time and the orchestrator decides where each runs, so a monitor must
not alarm every time an instance disappears because the scale was reduced —
the moving-target problem of Session 5; d describes the traditional case,
a and c are invented.

**Q7 — applied scenario** *(tests @sec-09-exercises · applied)* —
**Model answer:** The canary: a decoy credential or resource no legitimate
process should touch, e.g. a fake `admin_passwords.txt` file or an unused
decoy user account in Nextcloud. Why near-zero false positives: since no
legitimate process ever touches it, any interaction indicates an attempted
or actual breach (CSA, 2024, p. 142) — which directly answers the analysts'
false-positive problem. Path: the fast path, because a triggered canary is
high-risk activity where a fifteen-minute slow-path delay is too long;
events on the fast path are analysed and turned into alerts almost at once.
Same path: another key indicator such as management console logins without
MFA, any IAM policy change, use of the root account, or impossible-travel
logins — all management-plane/identity activity the Guidance names for
close, timely watching. **Grading notes:** full credit requires (1) a
plausible Nextcloud canary, (2) the no-legitimate-access argument for
near-zero false positives, (3) fast path with the timeliness justification,
and (4) one correct key indicator; partial credit for three of the four;
placing the canary on the slow path loses the timeliness point.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-09-event-vs-alert — Event vs alert)*
An event is anything that happens and can be recorded, mostly normal; an
alert is a message that demands attention, raised when events match a rule.
Because there are vastly more events than incidents, the value of monitoring
lies in filtering the many events down to the few meaningful alerts.

(2) *(@exr-09-telemetry-sources — The two key telemetry sources)*
Management plane logs (who accessed the infrastructure, what they did,
when) and service/application logs (authentication attempts, API access,
network traffic, service events). The management plane controls everything,
so losing it is the worst case; it must be watched so that an attacker there
is seen immediately.

(3) *(@exr-09-signature-vs-anomaly — Signature vs anomaly detection)*
Signature-based detection matches known attack
patterns; anomaly-based detection flags departures from normal. Anomaly
detection relies on the baseline, because abnormal is only defined against a
recorded picture of normal.

(4) *(@exr-09-fast-vs-slow — Fast path vs slow path)*
The fast path analyses events in near real
time for high-risk activity; the slow path handles logs with delay for
forensics. A suspicious management-plane action belongs on the fast path,
because a delay of minutes is too long for the highest-value target.

(5) *(@exr-09-canary-token — The canary token)*
A canary is a decoy no legitimate process should touch, so any access is
almost certainly malicious; for example a fake `admin_passwords.txt` or an
unused decoy user account in Nextcloud, whose every access raises a definite
alarm.
